1:
Calvin explains why a prophet turns chronicler. Jeremiah seems to take up the office of an historian, but he is sealing his earlier prophecies and showing he had brought nothing forward rashly; the chapter is the proof of all his former doctrine. He draws the moral from Zedekiah, exhorted again and again to surrender and obstinately refusing the yoke: fools become wise too late, never obeying good counsel while they may, and learning at last from their own miseries that what they despised was true, without any benefit from knowing it. Ellicott says only that the crisis came as Jeremiah had predicted, and judges the two opening verses inserted by the editor to explain how the previous chapter closed. Keil and Delitzsch reads the three verses as one period broken by a parenthesis on the duration of the siege, so that the sentence reaches its conclusion only when the princes come in.

The dates are converted for the reader. Gill and Wesley name the tenth month Tebeth, answering to part of December and part of January, so the siege began in winter; Clarke fixes it more nearly, the month beginning with the first new moon of our January and the city invested on its tenth day. For the fourth month Gill gives Tammuz. Clarke and Ellicott both make the siege eighteen months, ended by famine. Calvin dwells on what that meant: a city today bearing a few months of siege would be reckoned a rare instance of valour, and here were famine and pestilence, and a king who could watch men perish by scores and persist. Henry tells the siege with a slack middle: the army sat down in the depth of winter, the king soon retired to take his pleasure and left his generals, the work was intermitted and then renewed with redoubled vigour, until at midsummer they entered against soldiers too weakened by famine to resist. Jerusalem was so strong, he says, that nobody would have believed an enemy could enter its gates; but sin had provoked God to withdraw his protection, and then, like Samson when his hair was cut, it was weak as other cities.

Where the middle gate stood is guessed rather than known. Wesley and Henry place it in an inner wall dividing the city, and Henry explains the halt as caution, the generals not daring to press into so large a city until every place had been searched for an ambush. Clarke puts it in the valley between the two hills the city stood on, so that the Chaldeans, entering by the northern breach and posting themselves in the centre, became masters of the whole, while Zedekiah fled by the opposite gate. Ellicott reaches a similar position by the walls, between a citadel not yet surrendered and the lower city where the breach was made, and thinks the open space had been a forum, so that to encamp there was to assert mastery in the heart of the city. The names divide them further. Henry hears in their roughness what a sad change sin had made, since where Eliakim and Hilkiah once sat, bearing the name of the God of Israel, now sit men bearing the names of heathen gods; and he takes two of the six for titles. Clarke reduces the six to three, each name followed by its office, and suspects the first of the two identical names is an error for the general-in-chief, though he grants the point is as uncertain as it is unimportant. Ellicott treats each name as having its own meaning and history, one half an Assyrian deity called the great hero, another a Babylonian god, and one second word a title meaning chief eunuch. Calvin leaves it alone: whether a surname is added to some of them is of no great moment, and it is enough that the chief leaders are named, which accredits the narrative.
4:
Gill supposes the king and his soldiers watched the princes take the middle gate from some high tower where they had gone for safety. How they got out is guessed at: Clarke proposes a private underground passage. Ellicott is content with the gate itself, which opened from the garden of the palace and led toward the plain of the Jordan valley. Clarke explains the road: of the two ways from Jerusalem to Jericho the king took the plain rather than the one over the mount of Olives because it was quicker, probably meaning to cross the Jordan and escape to Egypt, whose people were then his allies. Ellicott supposes rather that he meant to take the ford and get away into the open country of Gilead. Calvin looks at who was left behind, and calls it a sad spectacle: men untrained for war, with women and children, remained while the men of war fled, their case the worse for having delayed the surrender. The ungodly, he says, flee when danger comes and are so filled with terror that they cast themselves into fresh perils; had the king come out as a suppliant he might have found mercy, and that counsel was given while things were not yet desperate.

Gill offers two accounts of how the pursuit began, either that deserters told of the flight or that the king was not found at the palace, and notes that only part of the army went, the rest staying to demolish the city. Calvin sees a hidden impulse from above. The plain was almost a desert, so finding one man in that solitude is a wonder unless God was their guide; he grants the king was probably betrayed by his own people, but insists he could have escaped had he not been given up. Clarke places Riblah on the northern frontier and Wesley on the borders of the land, Wesley adding the legal ground of the sentence, that Zedekiah was a tributary bound by covenant and oath. Ellicott gives the place its strategic sense: a town on the river from which the great trade routes ran toward Nineveh and Babylon and Egypt, a natural post of observation for a king whose generals were besieging elsewhere. Calvin explains the stay less kindly, that Nebuchadnezzar would not endure a long siege nor be near the danger, yet stayed close enough to keep the Jews in terror.

On the slaughter Gill notes that the king gave the order rather than striking himself, that some of the sons must have been very young since their father was only thirty-two, and that the bitterest part was knowing it came of his own obstinacy in refusing the prophet's advice. Ellicott observes that Eastern monarchies offer several examples of this refinement of cruelty. Calvin reads the killing of the nobles as policy rather than rage: with the royal family and every man of name destroyed, none was left capable of restoring the land, and every hope was cut off. On the blinding, Gill and Ellicott both find two prophecies fulfilled at once, that the king should see the king of Babylon and be carried there, and that he should not see the city he was carried to; Gill calls it a full proof of the prescience of God. Ellicott follows him into the dark, noting that nothing more is known of him, and that when his brother was released from that city twenty-six years later no mention is made of Zedekiah, from which it is natural to infer his sufferings had ended before. Calvin dwells on the deliberateness of it. The point of leaving him alive was that he should die by little and little, since death would have removed him from the miseries of this life; a man who had hardened himself against every truth had his punishment drawn out as long as his obstinacy had been.
8:
Gill and Ellicott both date the burning a month after the capture, and Ellicott adds that it was the work of the captain of the guard, sent once the city had fallen, and that the temple went with the palace. Calvin takes the verse as another seal on the prophecy. Jeremiah had said that if the king surrendered the houses would not be burnt; Zedekiah thought this vain or closed his ears, and now, blind, he heard that God had declared nothing in vain. He also notes that the singular house of the people stands for the plural, since the fire consumed not one house but all, and that the walls follow, so that the city was destroyed exactly as predicted.

The captain of the guard is identified by his title. Keil and Delitzsch renders it chief of the slayers, that is of the executioners, the head of the king's body-guard and first among the royal attendants; Ellicott gives the same sense, notes the title is given to a court officer in Genesis, and thinks it answered to a commander of the body-guard. Ellicott adds that he took no part in the siege but arrived a month after the capture to direct the destruction down to its details. Keil and Delitzsch pauses over a pronoun, since the deserters fall away to him with no antecedent in the context, though the parallel reads to the king of Babylon; he allows it might also be referred forward to the captain of the guard as the king's representative. Clarke calls them simply the deserters during the siege. Calvin looks at their motives. So great was the despair of many that they went over before the city fell, and these were the men Zedekiah had feared, lest he become an object of mockery to them if he surrendered. Why they too were carried off he explains two ways: either the conqueror could not confide in traitors who had broken faith with their own lawful king; or the removal was granted at their own request, since once the Chaldeans withdrew the common people would have raged against men who had helped the enemy, so that they might live quietly far away though not safely at home.

Why the poorest were left is answered practically by three voices and providentially by the fourth. Gill says they would have been no service but a burden, and there was nothing to fear from them, since they had no arms to rebel with and no money to buy any; besides, it was in the conqueror's interest that the land be worked rather than lie waste, so that tribute might come from it. Ellicott makes the same calculation from the other side, that giving the exiles' land to the poor would enlist their interest on the conqueror's side and keeping the soil in cultivation secured the tribute; and he adds that such wholesale deportation was the settled policy of the great Assyrian and Babylonian monarchs. Clarke is blunter, calling them the very refuse of the inhabitants, not worth carrying away, among whom the fields of the deported were divided. Calvin turns the arrangement into a lesson. The nobles had been killed and many of the middle sort had died in the siege, and the land was left to the poor alone, so that men who had not owned a foot of ground now lived comfortably, each with some extent of land because they were not many. It was better for them, he says, to have gone hungry a while and been trodden underfoot than to have lived in pomp; God often shows his care by not letting us rise high, and the issue proves at last that he had our salvation in view. And he sets the contrast plainly: the king led away bound and blind, the possessors of the land torn from it, the destitute left secure upon it.
11:
Henry marks the turn: here we must sing of mercy, as before of judgment. When Jerusalem lay in ruins and men's hearts failed for fear, this one man might lift up his head, knowing his redemption drew nigh. How the king came to know of him the voices agree on. Gill supposes it reached him through his generals, informed by deserters that Jeremiah had foretold the taking of the city, had pressed the king and princes to surrender, and had suffered much for it; and the Lord, he adds, put this regard into the heart of a monarch not otherwise disposed toward his prophets. Clarke and Wesley say the same. Ellicott allows the deserters, or Zedekiah himself, and raises the possibility that an earlier journey to the Euphrates had brought king and prophet into contact; from the captain's arrival he became an honoured counsellor.

Henry reads the order three ways. It was generous in a haughty potentate to take cognizance of one poor prophet, since it is the character of a great soul to notice the sufferings of the meanest; and the charge was given before the city fell and honourably kept in the heat of action. It was a reproach to Zedekiah and the princes, who put him in prison while the king of Babylon took him out, for God's ministers have often found fairer usage among strangers than among their own, as Paul found more favour with Agrippa than with Ananias. And it performed a promise, that God would cause the enemy to treat him well in the day of evil. Calvin turns to the danger. The innocent are often killed in a tumult, and even leaders cannot moderate the excesses of victors; when the palace burned, the prophet might have been suffocated or buried in the ruins. He instances the taking of Syracuse, where Marcellus wished Archimedes preserved for his noble genius, and yet a common soldier killed him as he drew his circles on the ground.

Gill spells out the charge: to look well to him is to take him out of prison and let him want for nothing, or, on the other rendering, to set thine eyes upon him and look pleasantly at him, keeping him in view rather than in neglect. Calvin grants that Nebuchadnezzar regarded only his own advantage, and makes that the point: the heathen king's mind was ruled by the secret power of God, who works in this way by the ungodly. It is not always by a voluntary act that men serve God, since many execute what he has decreed with no intention of it, being driven until they obey whether willing or not. The prophet never thought he owed his life to the king, Calvin adds, but knew he had been wonderfully preserved; and though he was in prison, his word was not bound.

Gill notices that sending to the prison was among the captain's first acts, the other princes joining in the commission. Ellicott identifies one from Assyrian records and thinks the name possibly another form of one already given. He also registers an apparent discrepancy, since the prophet is elsewhere set free at Ramah, and suggests he was sent back at first to the prison until he could be placed under protection. On the choice of protector Ellicott says the reason lies almost on the surface: Gedaliah came of a house that for three generations had stood by the prophets, his grandfather the king's scribe who helped restore the temple and first read the newly found law, his father the man who protected Jeremiah under an earlier king, and his uncle the one who lent him a chamber and tried to turn aside the king's wrath. Calvin gives the practical reason beside it: the princes knew the people hated the prophet, and committed him to that house not to be watched but to be kept from violence.
15:
Wesley notes that these four verses report something earlier than what precedes, and Gill dates the word before the city fell and after Ebedmelech had drawn the prophet out of the dungeon. Why it stands here Gill answers plainly: to show the regard the Lord has for those who show favour to his prophets. No account of the fulfilment survives, he admits, but he makes no doubt of it. Ellicott reasons to the same conclusion differently, that a prophet who sets down such a prediction knew it had been fulfilled; nothing more is heard of the faithful Ethiopian, but he was probably spared at the prophet's intercession. He notes too that the promise runs in the same terms as one made elsewhere to the prophet's scribe, and that the men Ebedmelech feared were the princes he had irritated by interfering for Jeremiah. Gill guards the opening command, since the prophet could not leave the prison; he was to acquaint the man with it as he had opportunity, by writing or by word of mouth.

Calvin makes the passage turn on who this man was. God was not unmindful of an alien from a barbarous nation, who alone dared take up a hopeless cause when others were terrified into silence, and roused both high and low against himself. Whatever we do for God's servants, Calvin says, God reckons as done to himself, as in the promise about a cup of cold water; and the Spirit set down this example to rouse us to the duties of humanity, and not to shun the hatred of men or the dangers we may incur. He hears in the repetition a reproof of the Jews, delivered in the person of a foreigner they despised as not of the holy seed, God regarding him while rejecting children of Abraham who were his only after the flesh.

The promise is timed as well as given. Calvin observes that it came before the city fell so that Ebedmelech might stay at home rather than flee with the king, and takes this for the design of all God's promises, to give quietness of mind; for when fear takes hold there is no settled purpose. He notes what the first half of the message secures. Had Jerusalem fallen by chance, Ebedmelech might justly have feared; told it would fall by God's just judgment, he could be sure of his safety, since the God who destroys a people can preserve one man. And the mention of the men he feared is not idle: he had shown an intrepid mind but was not divested of the feelings of nature, and the reminder made him readier to receive the promise, since God's blessings are reckoned at nothing until we know how necessary they are.

Gill records the Hebrew emphasis of the last verse, in delivering I will deliver thee, a repetition that confirms what went before. Calvin expounds the life given for a prey by comparison. Men count a small gain great when it comes beyond expectation; as men in a shipwreck throw out merchandise and money and think it enough to reach harbour, preferring to beg their bread rather than sink, so a man may count bare life a great gain though stripped of everything else. Calvin weighs why the reason given is trust rather than kindness. Another ground might have been named, that he reached out his hand to a holy man in extreme misery; but because that office of humanity proceeded from faith, God names the chief cause. Clarke says the same in a line: this man feared the Lord and not the king or his princes, and they who fear God need fear nothing besides. Henry draws the rule: God recompenses men's services according to their principles, and those who trust him in the way of duty find their hope does not fail in the time of greatest danger.
